items.title: Toward an integrative theoretical model of AI-supported cybersecurity governance and organizational resilience
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports cybersecurity work through risk scoring, anomaly detection, alert triage, vulnerability prioritization, threat-intelligence enrichment, and incident-response assistance. Existing research explains important aspects of technical performance, responsible AI, cybersecurity oversight, and organizational decision-making, but it still provides limited explanation of how AI-generated analytical outputs become admissible, reviewable, and actionable within formal cybersecurity decision processes. This conceptual article develops the construct of AI-supported decision structures: the organizational arrangements through which AI-generated cybersecurity inputs are assessed for reliability and context, governed through use rules and escalation paths, embedded in recurring governance routines, connected to accountable decision ownership, and subjected to substantive human oversight. The article differentiates this construct from adjacent concepts in IS governance, AI governance, algorithmic management, human oversight, and digital surveillance governance. It also introduces theoretical tension by showing that stronger governance structures may improve decision quality and legitimacy while also creating trade-offs such as slower response, procedural overload, surveillance expansion, and symbolic compliance. The article develops a conceptual model and five mechanism-based propositions linking AI-supported decision structures to cybersecurity decision quality, decision legitimacy, coordinated response, and organizational resilience understood through anticipation, coping, and adaptation. The contribution is integrative rather than a claim of complete novelty: the framework recontextualizes established governance ideas around a distinct object of governance, namely AI-generated analytical inputs that shape cybersecurity judgment before formal authority is exercised.

items.title: Toward Culturalized Generative AI for the Creative and Cultural Industries: Lessons from Adaptive Cultural Mediation
items.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary generative AI systems are not yet consistently equipped to provide the level of culturalization required in the creative and cultural industries (CCIs). Debates on generative AI in cultural domains have focused primarily on productivity, innovation, intellectual property, labor disruption and bias. While these concerns are important, they do not fully capture a more basic issue: cultural production depends on forms of meaning that are historically situated, socially mediated and unevenly distributed across languages, communities and markets. In such contexts, fluency, safety and technical usefulness are not sufficient measures of system quality. The paper discusses how an existing line of thought from localization, cross-cultural design and culturalization research should be carried into the era of generative AI as explicit attention to cultural context, symbolic meaning and interpretive plurality. The CCIs provide a particularly revealing testbed for this claim because they expose limitations of generic AI evaluation in domains where value depends on tone, memory, symbolism and representation. The argument combines published evidence on cultural bias and uneven representation in contemporary models with diagnostic case studies using ChatGPT 5.5 in museums, heritage sites and pilgrimage contexts. These studies illustrate concrete cultural-mediation problems under the conditions tested. On that basis, the article proposes a framework for culturalized generative AI and outlines an integrated research and governance agenda spanning AI, the humanities and cultural-sector practice.

items.title: TRACE: Tackling Real-World Resource Assignment Problems via Agentic Heuristic Design
items.abstract: Dynamic resource assignment, the real-time allocation of task streams to heterogeneous processing nodes, is the backbone of modern computing infrastructure. While learning-based schedulers excel in research, industrial deployments still rely on hand-written rules that operators can read, audit, and execute within tight latency budgets. LLM-based Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) promises to automate writing such rules. However, existing AHD frameworks were developed for combinatorial problems fully specified to the LLM, and they learn only from a scalar fitness score. In real systems, the behaviour that determines a good heuristic, such as processor speeds or power consumption, is unknown a priori: the score reveals which heuristic performs better, but not why. This missing information is recorded in the system logs that every evaluation produces. Exploiting it is non-trivial: logs are massive and noisy, the relevant signals depend on the objective, and their content and format vary across hardware and software stacks, so they can neither be fed to an LLM as is nor processed by a fixed parser. We propose TRACE, which couples an evolutionary AHD loop with an agentic knowledge-extraction workflow. A Reasoner agent analyzes the log schema in light of the objective and formulates hypotheses about the system dynamics; a Coder agent writes and executes schema-specific code to test them, producing insights or executable tools for the evolved heuristics. We evaluate TRACE on a synthetic cloud benchmark and a 5G vRAN scenario built from industrial testbed measurements and operational traffic traces. TRACE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art AHD methods in resource assignment problems and yields more auditable heuristics at under 2% overhead.

items.title: Turkish Adaptation of the AI Motivation Scale (AIMS): A Self-Determination Theory Approach
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has underscored the need to better understand students’ motivation to learn with AI. Motivation is a key determinant of students’ engagement and effective use of AI-supported learning environments; however, there is a scarcity of validated instruments grounded in robust motivational theory and adapted to different cultural contexts. Recently, the Artificial Intelligence Motivation Scale (AIMS), based on Self-Determination Theory, was developed to assess university students’ motivation to learn with AI across five dimensions: intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation. The present study aims to adapt the AIMS into Turkish and to examine its validity and reliability among Turkish university students. The study sample consisted of 221 undergraduate and graduate students from 10 universities in Türkiye. Following a translation and back-translation procedure, the Turkish version of the AIMS was administered online. The factorial structure of the scale was examined using first- and second-order confirmatory factor analyses, and internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. The results supported the original five-factor structure and demonstrated acceptable model fit and satisfactory reliability coefficients. The second-order analysis provided partial support for a higher-order AI motivation construct. Overall, the findings indicate that the Turkish version of the AIMS is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing university students’ motivation to learn with AI in the Turkish education context.

items.title: Uncanny Valley in Conversation? Effects of Internal and External Human-Likeness on Intimacy and Trust
items.abstract: Conversational agents built on large language models increasingly converse like humans, expressing emotions and disclosing their own experiences. Human-likeness, however, has been studied largely as a matter of appearance—how human an agent looks. Language now also lets an agent display internal human-likeness by conveying an inner life, raising the question of how deeply an AI should express its own experiences—and whether that depends on its appearance. In a 2 (appearance: machine-like vs. human-like) × 3 (self-disclosure: none vs. low vs. high) between-subjects experiment, 193 university students completed a single, brief, fully scripted counseling session with an AI counselor prototype and evaluated it on six measures, controlling for prior mind perception. The effects of disclosure depth depended on appearance: with the machine-like counselor, intimacy and social presence peaked at low and declined at high disclosure, with trust and perceived authenticity showing the same direction—an uncanny valley-like pattern—whereas with the human-like counselor evaluations generally rose with depth. Deeper disclosure was not judged more inappropriate, and moderated mediation analyses showed that deepening disclosure from low to high reduced anthropomorphism—and, through it, intimacy and trust—only for the machine-like counselor. Internal and external human-likeness were read together: how deeply an AI should speak about itself cannot be decided apart from how it looks.

items.title: Understanding Learner Engagement and Persistence in AI-Assisted Interactive Climate Fiction Learning
items.abstract: Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled educators to create increasingly sophisticated interactive learning materials, yet relatively little research has examined how learners engage with and persist in such interventions over time. This exploratory case study investigated learner engagement and persistence within a five-stage AI-assisted interactive climate fiction (cli-fi) intervention delivered through H5P activities embedded within the Moodle learning management system as part of an extracurricular sustainability initiative at an English-medium university in China. Participation, activity scores, completion data, and time-on-task measures were analysed descriptively across a five-week intervention. While learners who engaged with the intervention demonstrated high levels of engagement, reflected in strong activity scores and substantial interaction with the materials, participation declined markedly across successive stages, falling from 25 learners in Story 1 to six learners by Story 5. Descriptive improvements were observed in environmental knowledge scores among the small number of learners completing both pre- and post-tests, although these findings were inconclusive. The findings highlight a clear distinction between engagement and persistence, suggesting that engaging digital learning experiences do not necessarily translate into sustained participation. The study contributes to emerging research on AI-assisted learning design by emphasising the importance of considering persistence as a distinct outcome when designing and evaluating multi-stage digital learning environments.

items.title: Unpacking AI Agent Participation in Issue-Centered Collaboration in Open-Source Software Development
items.abstract: The increasing participation of AI agents in open-source software development raises questions about their role in collaborative processes. This paper investigates how AI agent participation relates to the structure and outcomes of issue-centered collaboration in open-source software projects. We adopt a process-level perspective by modeling issue handling as sequences of events and extending dynamic issue-pr entropy to distinguish between agent-related and non-agent-related contributions. Using large-scale issue event data from 83 GitHub repositories, we construct a project–month panel dataset and analyze associations between collaboration complexity and development outcomes. Our results show that agent-related collaboration complexity is more strongly associated with development output than human-only collaboration complexity, and is associated with fewer newly introduced defects. In contrast, its relationship with issue resolution efficiency is highly context-dependent. These findings highlight the importance of considering collaboration structure when evaluating the impact of AI agents in open-source software development.

items.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Automated Warfare: The Israel - Gaza Conflict
items.abstract: The fact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly integrated into military systems has transformed the modern warfare and changed approaches, tactics, and ethical perspectives. This paper will look at the application of AI in automatic warfare with a special consideration of the Israel-gaza war. It examines the ways in which the use of AI-based technologies by Israel, such as autonomous drones, predictive targeting software, and algorithmic surveillance systems have revolutionized the efficiency of combat and intelligence activities. The history provides insights into the globalization of AI into the military and its consequences to international security, humanitarian law, and ethics. As the problem statement indicates, it lacks proper legal frameworks and accountability mechanisms that can be used to regulate the use of AI in lethal operations, especially in the civilian-populated area like Gaza. The literature review has summarized the academic views on dual nature; as a strategic benefit and a humanitarian threat of AI. It talks about the way AI increases accuracy, speed, and the situational awareness and at the same time brings new challenges of transparency, bias on algorithms and ethical accountability. Also, in the review, it is noted that AI-assisted systems may help to minimize operational risks to soldiers, though they may be harmful to civilians when there is no meaningful human control over their use. The analysis is qualitative, as it crucially makes use of secondary data such as policy reports, human rights organizations, and peer-reviewed scholarly publications on the topic to investigate ethical, legal, and operational aspects of the use of AI in warfare. The results indicate that despite the fact that AI has advanced the military intelligence and targeting capabilities of Israel, it has also led to the increase of the issues of accountability, proportionality, as well as the violation of human rights. The conclusion underlines the necessity of the international legal tools, ethical principles, and control tools in order to govern the military application of AI. It has been recommended in a policy that there be transparency, substantial human intervention, and international collaboration to guarantee that AI technologies are used to address the ideals of humanity and global peace

items.title: Using artificial intelligence to mitigate global teacher shortage
items.abstract: Purpose This viewpoint addresses the systemic global teacher crisis – driven by burnout, unsustainable workloads and administrative attrition – and explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to reduce non-academic tasks. This piece argues that by using AI to help with administrative burdens, education systems can improve teacher retention, enhance individual student engagement and even support democracy. Design/methodology/approach This piece uses a conceptual and synthesis-based approach, combining a review of current literature with the author's firsthand narrative reflections as a veteran educator and teacher trainer. Findings The piece identifies the root causes of the teacher shortage: the overwhelming volume of non-instructional work. The analysis of the literature supports the use of AI tools to unburden teachers from non-instructional work gaining time to build robust relationships with students, increase the individualization of instruction, all of which can lead to better meeting the learning needs of their students. Finally, it allows for a better life–work balance that can mitigate teacher attrition and attract more quality candidates. Research limitations/implications This is a viewpoint article, and although it is supported by a robust review of relevant literature, it does not put forward new empirical evidence. Practical implications The practical implications of the piece focus on reforming the daily operations of educators' work by integrating AI to eliminate up to six hours of administrative workload per week, thereby reducing teacher burnout and mitigating the global shortage. Social implications The social implications center on safeguarding democratic foundations by stabilizing an endangered education system. Restoring work–life balance through AI helps attract and retain qualified teachers, preventing the systemic collapse of public schooling. Originality/value The originality of this piece is in its unique view of how to mitigate the teacher shortage by embracing AI tools rather than fear them. By using relevant national and international literature in conjunction with the authentic, lived perspective of a veteran educator, the piece provides a fresh approach to combatting the teacher shortage.

items.title: What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?
items.abstract: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

items.title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
items.abstract: Generative AI can support writing, but frictionless access may cause cognitive offloading before users develop their own ideas. We introduce Engage-to-Unlock, a productive-friction mechanism that unlocks generative capabilities after users meaningfully engage with the task. In a controlled experiment (N = 398), participants completed a writing task under one of four conditions: Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, Engage-to-Unlock, or Time-Matched Unlock, which matched unlock timing to Engage-to-Unlock participants but independent of users' engagement, then evaluated passages for evidence and inferential errors. Results show that Engage-to-Unlock redistributed effort across tasks: participants spent more time writing and less time evaluating, without increasing overall task duration. They also submitted more prompts than in other AI-assisted conditions and showed the highest accuracy-per-time evaluation efficiency across conditions. These findings suggest that designing GenAI access to encourage early human engagement may provide a productive form of friction, while retaining active AI use and efficient downstream evaluation.

items.title: Workplace responses to perpetration of family and domestic violence: a global scoping review
items.abstract: Introduction Family and domestic violence (FDV), which includes intimate partner and family violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace interventions addressing the issue of FDV have predominantly concentrated on providing support to victim-survivors, while there is limited research regarding employer responses to employees who perpetrate such violence. Method A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources, and 28 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Practical applications Effective workplace responses to perpetration of FDV should consider work design factors, referral pathways and confidentiality protections which are guided by graduated accountability models and regulatory frameworks.

items.title: Zenodo Metadata — Be: Founding Business Proposal v2.0
items.abstract: Be is a proposed organization dedicated to making safe, professionally governed artificial intelligence emotional support freely accessible to people who need someone to talk to. Be proposes an AI emotional-support system designed around a foundational distinction: an AI must never confuse what it observes with what it infers. Version 2.0 further develops the proposal's framework for adaptive conversational communication through the principle Adaptive Tone, Fixed Boundaries. Be may adapt its tone, vocabulary, pacing, humor, warmth, and conversational style to meet an individual where they are, while maintaining fixed ethical and relational boundaries. The system should allow human-like communication without creating a false human identity, adapting the interface without fabricating the relationship. The proposal incorporates Red Tape Theory™ as a proposed safety methodology: Observe. Record. Question. Do not force the axiom. Interpretation must never be represented as observation. Be does not propose to diagnose users or replace licensed mental-health professionals. Instead, it proposes a professionally governed pathway through which an AI system may recognize when AI-only support may no longer be an appropriate level of support and facilitate access to human care. A proposed charitable human-care program, If You Get It, You Get It, would seek to use charitable resources to help people access licensed professional care when professionally established safety criteria indicate that additional human support may be appropriate. Version 2.0 expands the proposal's treatment of personalization as a safety boundary, including the distinction between adapting communication to an individual and constructing a misleading simulated relationship. It also addresses clinical governance, privacy, autonomy, human handoff, crisis safety, documentation, intellectual-property considerations, research and evaluation, and a potential future child-focused system provisionally called NewBee. This publication is a founding proposal and does not represent a deployed clinical service, licensed mental-health treatment program, clinical efficacy claim, professional endorsement, or completed charitable program. Be begins with the question: Where could this harm somebody?

items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of digital technologies has transformed modern society in almost every sphere of human life. The growth of the internet, smartphones, social media, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data, digital payments, e-commerce, and online education has created what is commonly described as a digital society. Digital technologies have improved communication, access to information, education, healthcare, business, public administration, and economic participation. At the same time, the increasing dependence on digital systems has created significant ethical challenges relating to privacy, data protection, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, misinformation, digital inequality, online harassment, intellectual property, surveillance, and the responsible use of emerging technologies.

items.title: A federated explainable artificial intelligence architecture for multimodal disaster intelligence and response coordination
items.abstract: Natural disasters demand rapid synthesis of fragmented, heterogeneous data often distributed across independently governed organizations. This paper introduces DisasterAI, a federated, cloud-native, and multi-modal AI architecture for disaster intelligence. Unlike centralized analytics platforms, DisasterAI emphasizes federated data ingestion, modular adapters, and the alignment of derived intelligence—enabling cross-agency coordination without requiring raw data consolidation. The architecture integrates satellite imagery (optical and SAR), IoT sensor streams, public alerts, and contextual civic data into a unified, explainable decision-support pipeline. DisasterAI addresses critical challenges in disaster intelligence, including spatial-temporal alignment of asynchronous data, modality-aware fusion, uncertainty representation, and fairness-aware decision-making. Designed to support the entire disaster lifecycle—from early warning and forecast-informed risk analysis to impact assessment and response prioritization—it operates within a human-in-the-loop decision-support context. A scenario-driven evaluation illustrates how DisasterAI enhances coordination effectiveness, improves prioritization consistency, and maintains robustness under partial data availability. By focusing on architectural behavior and operational integration rather than algorithmic benchmarking, this work positions federated, explainable AI systems as a viable foundation for scalable and reliable disaster-response frameworks in complex, data-constrained environments.

items.title: A framework for institutional change in the age of AI
items.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping STEM higher education. Not only are our educational practices changing, but how we think about educational transformation must also adapt. Existing models of institutional change in STEM, aimed at interactive engagement, have largely followed an adoption logic: relatively stable, well-researched educational practices are evaluated and then scaled. These assumptions do not hold for generative AI, which is an arrival technology – entering classrooms before a sufficient pedagogical evidence base could form, and requiring institutions to act under uncertainty. Building on recent decades of work on STEM education institutional change, we propose a framework identifying six dimensions along which prior models of change must be adapted in light of AI: three concerning the tools at the center of reform (the tool’s evidence base, rate of change, and scope), and three concerning the people involved in change (faculty, change agents, and students). For each dimension, we examine how AI-era assumptions differ from those underlying prior STEM education reforms and derive design implications, including: privileging humble and local inquiries; organizing reform around pedagogical approaches rather than specific tools; repositioning change agents as facilitators of collective inquiry; and engaging students as partners in reform. Collectively, the six dimensions and design implications constitute a framework for adapting change models to support institutions under conditions of genuine uncertainty. Finally, we illustrate how the framework may be applied through a brief case-study of a faculty workshop series carried out in a university physics department to support instructors adapting to this modern AI era.

items.title: A pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework for human-autonomy teaming in future fighter aviation
items.abstract: Future fighter operations are expected to combine increasingly capable autonomy, collaborative aircraft, dense sensor information, and sustained physiological and cognitive demands. This Perspective proposes a pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework in which the pilot, a pilot-specific digital twin, an intelligent flight-management system, the aircraft, and external agents are treated as interdependent elements within a systems-of-systems framework. The framework does not replace situation awareness, distributed cognition, joint cognitive systems, adaptive automation, or human-autonomy teaming. Instead, it extends their unit of analysis by making the pilot’s dynamic physiological and neurocognitive state, longitudinal variability, and health-related constraints explicit system variables and design objectives. The pilot digital twin is defined narrowly as an individualized state-estimation and forecasting capability, whereas the intelligent flight-management system integrates pilot, platform, mission, and environmental information to provide explainable recommendations and, where authorized, bounded adaptive action. We identify testable propositions concerning individualized prediction, adaptive support, shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and governance. The framework is prospective and requires validation in simulation, training, and operationally representative environments. Its purpose is to organize research toward systems that protect pilot agency, sustain performance, and preserve long-term health while exploiting increasingly autonomous teammates.

items.title: A Preliminary Evaluation of the e-Learning for Renal Applied Pharmacology Tool for Enhancing Pharmacology Learning: A Pilot Quasi-Experimental Study
items.abstract: Electronic learning (e-learning) or online learning in medical education has become increasingly prevalent, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, poor student engagement and reduced motivation are among the critical challenges associated with online learning. The e-learning for Renal Applied Pharmacology (e-RAP) is a new technology-enhanced learning tool that includes a nephron image augmented with several Quick Response (QR) codes. It allows students to access relevant QR-linked educational materials prepared by the teachers. This quasi-experimental pilot study examined whether use of the e-RAP tool was associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation among 105 preclinical medical students at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA), Malaysia. Participants in the intervention group (Year 2, n = 45) used the e-RAP tool, while the control group (Year 1, n = 60) received conventional teaching. Cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation scores were measured using pre- and posttest multiple-choice questions (MCQ), the Burch Engagement Survey for Students, and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, respectively. Both groups demonstrated improvements in mean cognitive scores from pre- to post-test MCQ, with greater gains in the intervention group than in the control group. The intervention group was also associated with higher emotional and cognitive engagement (both in and out of class) and higher scores in several motivational domains, including intrinsic value, cognitive strategy use, and selfregulation. Although groups differed by academic year, baseline knowledge was comparable. Taken together, these preliminary findings suggest that e-RAP use may be associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation.

items.title: A PROGNOSIS OF THE ETHICAL IMPERATIVES OF AI IN PREDICTIVE INTELLIGENCE AND MILITARY OPERATIONS IN AFRICA
items.abstract: The evolving dynamics of security management have necessitated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. This integration presents a paradigm of significant opportunities alongside profound challenges. Theoretically, AI promises to enhance situational awareness, enable results-oriented conflict management, and optimize operational efficiency across the continent. However, this study posits that its deployment is fraught with daunting ethical and practical impediments specific to the African context. This work interrogates the ethical imperatives of AI in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. To achieve its objectives—which include defining context-specific ethical principles, diagnosing implementation barriers, and proposing a practical framework—the study adopted a mixed-methods approach. This methodology relied on semi-structured interviews with military personnel, defence analysts, and AI ethics scholars, complemented by a historicist content analysis of secondary sources including policy documents, institutional reports, and academic literature. The findings reveal a strong consensus among stakeholders on the paramount importance of ethical principles such as accountability, transparency, fairness, and meaningful human oversight. However, the study identified that the realisation of these principles is severely constrained by critical obstacles, including a stark infrastructure and data deficit, a pervasive regulatory and policy vacuum, and pre-existing governance frailties. These contextual challenges amplify ethical risks, particularly algorithmic bias and accountability gaps, threatening to exacerbate social divisions and undermine human security. Consequently, the study concludes that ethically responsible AI use is not an automatic outcome but must be actively cultivated. It recommends, among other measures, the urgent development of a continent-wide regulatory framework by the African Union to harmonise standards and prevent misuse. The study argues that only through such deliberate, multi-faceted interventions—combining robust regulation, strategic investment in digital infrastructure, and international collaboration on equitable terms—can Africa harness the benefits of AI for security while safeguarding fundamental ethical imperatives.

items.title: A Situational Awareness-Driven Human-Machine Interface Framework for Enhancing Operators’ Performance in Agricultural Robotic Teleoperation
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing adoption of automated/autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs) in precision agriculture, existing human-machine interfaces (HMIs) remain function-centric, frequently neglecting the cognitive and user experience (UX) needs of non-technical operators. Consequently, current dashboards suffer from limited usability, high cognitive load, and reduced system transparency, increasing the risk of operator error. To address this gap within agricultural teleoperation interface design, this study presents a theory-driven HMI framework that systematically translates Endsley’s Situational Awareness (SA) theory (Perception, Comprehension, Projection) and ISO 9241 ergonomic principles into a structured three-panel AGV teleoperation interface. Unlike conventional function-oriented dashboards, the proposed framework organises interface components according to operator cognitive requirements to support information perception, comprehension, and projection during remote operation. A theory-driven agricultural teleoperation HMI framework was developed by translating cognitive and ergonomic principles into practical interface organization strategies. To formatively evaluate this SA-driven design architecture, we conducted a user-perception study with non-expert digitally literate participants (N = 20), evaluating three iterative HMI prototypes. The comparative results indicate that the SA-aligned layout received higher user ratings in perceived decision-support capability (SA3), cognitive workload reduction, and overall usability compared with baseline designs during formative evaluation. The study provides preliminary methodological guidance for agricultural teleoperation HMI design, while recognizing that objective operational validation with target agricultural users remains necessary.

items.title: A study on the relationship between teacher feedback types, self-efficacy, and intrinsic motivation among violin learners
items.abstract: Introduction To explore the psychological mechanisms of persistence in adult instrumental learning, this study investigates the associations among different types of teacher feedback, self-efficacy, and intrinsic motivation, and examines the moderating role of learning stages. Methods Using a cross-sectional survey design, scale and open-ended text data were collected from 743 adult violin learners. A moderated mediation model was tested through multiple regression and the Bootstrap method, supplemented by thematic analysis to provide a qualitative context. Results Data analysis indicates: (1) Positive feedback and constructive feedback are significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001; β = 0.342, p < 0.001), while negative feedback shows a significant negative association ( β = −0.318, p < 0.001); (2) Self-efficacy demonstrates a significant partial mediating association between the three types of feedback and intrinsic motivation, with indirect effect estimates of 0.103, 0.098, and −0.097, respectively (95% CIs all exclude 0); (3) The learning stage significantly moderates the conditional indirect effects: as the learning stage advances, the indirect association of positive feedback on intrinsic motivation via self-efficacy gradually weakens (index of moderated mediation = −0.045), whereas the indirect association of constructive feedback gradually strengthens (index of moderated mediation = 0.038). Open-ended texts echo these statistical paths at the micro-level. Discussion The study shows that there are heterogeneous and dynamic statistical connections between teacher feedback and adult intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy is a key pathway to understanding this connection. In practice, the provision of instructional feedback content should match the learners’ experience stage.

items.title: A Taxonomy of Human-AI Interaction Patterns in Agent-Based Operations Management
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing deployment of AI agents in operations management, spanning production scheduling, predictive maintenance, supply chain management, and energy systems, is progressively shifting automated systems from decision support tools to autonomous decision-making entities. Despite this transition, existing frameworks do not adequately characterize how humans and AI agents interact in operational decision-making contexts. This paper proposes a taxonomy of human-AI interaction patterns in agent-based operations management, developed through a theory-driven approach based on decision theory, control systems, human factors, and explainable AI research. The taxonomy articulates the interaction space along five analytically separable dimensions: Decision Trigger, Execution Authority, Human Entry Point, Human Influence and Interpretive Access. It identifies seven interaction patterns organized into four macro-patterns ordered by increasing AI operational autonomy. Illustrative examples drawn from scientific literature demonstrate the discriminative capacity of the taxonomy across heterogeneous operations management domains and agent architectures. The taxonomy provides researchers with an analytical instrument to characterize and compare human-AI decision loop configurations, and practitioners with a design reference for deliberate and accountable interaction choices in operational AI deployments.

items.title: Adoption Frequencies of Expert- Driven Learning-Based AI Taxonomy among R&D SMEs and Start-ups in Turkiye
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is widely studied at the organizational level, yet much less is known about the specific algorithms organizations adopt and the reasons for these choices. This study investigates AI adoption among research-and-development (R&D) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups in Turkiye through a proposed expert-driven, learning-domain-based taxonomy comprising 28 algorithms grouped into seven AI families. Survey data were collected from 36 organizations affiliated with the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce. Reliability and validity were established, and adoption was examined through descriptive statistics and non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests. At the algorithm level, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, Multilayer Perceptron, and Linear Regression were the most adopted, reflecting a preference for interpretable, structurally familiar methods, whereas Deep Q-Network, Policy Gradient, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping were the least adopted. At the family level, Unsupervised Learning and Natural Language Processing ranked highest, while Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Behavior recorded the lowest and most divergent adoption. Adoption also varied by sector—Financial/FinTech and Engineering/Defense showed the broadest portfolios and Healthcare and Commerce/e-Commerce the narrowest—with statistically significant cross-sector differences for Autonomous Behavior and Unsupervised Learning. Adoption range increased across organizational stages, peaking at post-incubation. The findings extend the Technology-Organization-Environment framework with diffusion of innovation and dynamic capability theory to the algorithm level and emphasize AI algorithms’ knowledge as a target for SMEs’ digital transformation.

This paper delves into the transformative power of AI in educational assessment and suggests a strategic framework for embracing digital change. By reviewing current literature, the study highlights AI-driven innovations like adaptive testing, automated grading, learning analytics, and competency-based assessment models. The paper emphasizes that a comprehensive, policy-oriented, and pedagogically sound approach are crucial for effectively integrating AI into assessment systems. In the end, it offers practical strategies for institutions aiming to update their assessment practices in an AI-enhanced educational environment.

items.title: AI Across Educational Levels
items.abstract: Primary education represents the foundational stage of formal education, where children develop essential academic, cognitive, social, emotional, creative, and communication skills. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into primary education offers new possibilities for personalized learning, interactive instruction, educational games, language development, accessibility, formative assessment, and teacher support. However, the use of AI at the primary level requires particular care because young learners may have limited ability to understand technological risks, evaluate AI-generated information, or protect their personal information independently. Therefore, AI should be introduced in an age-appropriate, safe, inclusive, and teacher-guided manner. The fundamental principle of AI in primary education is: Child → Teacher Guidance → AI-Supported Learning → Interaction → Feedback → Learning AI should support the educational process rather than replace teachers, parents, classroom interaction, play, creativity, or children's independent thinking.Artificial Intelligence in primary education refers to the use of AI-enabled technologies to support teaching, learning, assessment, educational communication, and the overall development of young learners. AI applications can provide personalized learning activities, interactive exercises, intelligent tutoring, language support, educational games, automated feedback, and assistive learning facilities. Examples of AI applications in primary education include intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, educational chatbots, speech-recognition applications, AI-supported language-learning systems, educational games, automated feedback tools, and AI-assisted teaching resources. The main purpose of AI at this level is to enhance the learning experience while keeping the teacher and the learner at the centre of education.

items.title: AI agents for decision support in logistics management: a literature review
items.abstract: The increasing complexity, volatility, and sustainability pressures affecting global supply chains have accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in logistics management. Among these AI approaches, Intelligent Agents (IAs) and Multi-agent Systems (MAS) have emerged as essential tools for supporting decentralized, adaptive, event-driven, and real-time decision-making processes in dynamic logistics environments. Unlike traditional centralized planning systems, agent-based approaches enable autonomous entities such as suppliers, warehouses, transportation units, and distribution centers to coordinate actions, exchange information, and manage variability. This paper presents a structured literature review of peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science on the use of AI agents to support decision-making in logistics management and supply chain operations. Particular attention is given to the strategic importance of intelligent agents in strengthening resilience, operational efficiency, and sustainability in increasingly uncertain logistics systems. The findings indicate that intelligent agents improve decision quality, responsiveness, coordination, and resource utilization across distributed logistics networks. Furthermore, Multi-Agent Systems enhance interoperability and collaboration among logistics actors, enabling more agile and resilient supply chains. However, challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, governance, scalability, and human–AI collaboration continue to limit large-scale implementation in industrial environments.

items.title: AI and Responsible Innovation: Technology, Society and Governance in the Technorapid Age for Viksit Bharat 2047.
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is getting integrated into the day-to-day life of every human being. This fast-changing technology is transforming traditional technology, society and governance at a rapid pace. This paper explores the emerging Technorapid Age, where technological change may move faster than the ability of individuals, institutions and governance systems to adapt. It focuses on Responsible Innovation as a methodology to manage this growing gap. It proposes that AI development should not be measured only by technological progress. It should also consider human well-being, social inclusion, ethical responsibility and effective governance. It examines the relationship between AI, technology and society. It highlights the need for human adaptability, accountability and responsible decision-making. The author proposes that Responsible Innovation can help create an equilibrium between technological acceleration and human adaptive capacity. The paper directly connects with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. India needs technological development that is innovative, inclusive, ethical and sustainable. Technology should support human dignity, social well-being and the needs of future generations. The research concludes that achieving Viksit Bharat 2047 requires comprehensive and responsible AI technologies. These innovations should benefit all sections of society (सर्वजन हिताय, सर्वजन सुखाय) and ensure that people are skilled and supported to handle challenges of the Technorapid Age.

items.title: AI Ethics Integrated with Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam for Viksit Bharat @2047
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of India's digital transformation. It is expected to impact governance, education, healthcare, finance, employment and everyday life as India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. However, this rapid development and adoption of technology also creates a growing gap between technological progress and the ability of individuals and society to adapt. This paper describes this condition as Technorapid, an accelerating pace of technological change that can exceed human, social, institutional and ethical adaptive capacity. The paper proposes that digital transformation should not remain confined to policies and institutional documents. Its success should ultimately be visible on the ground, in the lived experience of its citizens. AI-driven development needs to be evaluated through its ability to improve access, dignity, inclusion, education, employment and quality of life. This paper explores Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the principle that the world is one family, as a philosophical foundation for a human-centered approach to AI ethics. It argues that India's technological progress should be complemented by human adaptation, ethical governance and mechanisms that ensure that the benefits of AI reach diverse sections of society. The paper concludes that the true measure of Viksit Bharat @2047 should not be how advanced India's technologies become, but how meaningfully those technologies improve human live and national progress

items.title: AI Literacy for Higher Education: Responsible AI Use in Research, Thesis Writing, and Academic Reporting
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI) tools, in higher education has created significant opportunities in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting processes, while also raising important questions regarding academic integrity, accuracy, ethical responsibility, and human oversight. To promote informed and responsible use of AI while benefiting from the opportunities it offers, this study presents a framework for the ethical, critical, and responsible use of AI in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting in higher education. AI literacy is conceptualized not merely as the ability to use AI tools, but as the competence to evaluate and verify AI-generated information, establish ethical boundaries, and maintain academic responsibility. The study is designed as a narrative literature review and thematic evaluation based on academic studies and policy and guidance documents published by international organizations. The literature is examined in the contexts of AI literacy, generative AI, research ethics, academic integrity, thesis writing, source verification, and academic reporting. The findings indicate that AI can be used as a supportive tool in academic processes; however, scientific evaluation, source verification, methodological decision-making, and ultimate academic responsibility should remain with humans. The study argues that responsible AI use in higher education should be grounded in the principles of human oversight, critical thinking, verification, transparency, data privacy, and academic integrity. Accordingly, AI literacy should be regarded not merely as a technological skill but as a fundamental component of future academic and research competencies in higher education. items.title: AI Revolution: The Death of Business Administration and the Birth of Inalienable Leadership
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly performing administrative, analytical, coordinating, monitoring, communication, and decision-support functions historically associated with managers and business administration. This transformation does not imply the disappearance of organizations, management, managers, or business schools. It marks the erosion of administration as an exclusively human domain and as the principal justification for managerial authority. When machines can analyze, plan, coordinate, evaluate, recommend, and execute, leadership must be grounded in something deeper than superior control of information and process. Existing leadership theories explain traits, skills, behaviors, relationships, ethics, adaptation, collective agency, technological mediation, and organizational effectiveness. The documented review nevertheless identifies a higher-order question that these traditions do not make their central organizing principle: who retains final authority and responsibility over purposes, institutions, and civilizational direction when machines increasingly participate in organizational and social decision-making? This conceptual, theoretical, normative, and integrative working paper introduces and timestamps Inalienable Leadership as the first metatheory of leadership specifically formulated for the age of artificial intelligence and robotics, advances it as the overarching metatheory of leadership in that age, and formally records it as the twelfth and culminating original contribution of the complete FILE contribution system. FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution remains the core management theory and diagnostic framework. Its place within the broader leadership architecture is expressed by the formula Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment, with Intelligence conceptualized through FILE, Character through SQL, and Judgment through LENS. Inalienable Leadership integrates, grounds, governs, and gives civilizational direction to FILE and the complete FILE contribution system. The paper establishes a three-level hierarchy: Inalienable Leadership; the FILE Architecture (including the five meta-intelligences, the nested intelligences, and the Five Emergent Outcomes, which are products of the integrated exercise of FILE + SQL + LENS); and the first eleven original contributions and their associated structures. It preserves the specific roles of Human Irreducibility, HACK, HTTPS, LENS, MAIL, MLT, and RC while placing them under one civilizational principle: humanity may share work and intelligence with machines, but it cannot surrender its final authority and responsibility for the purposes, institutions, and direction of civilization. The future will not be determined by what machines can do, but by whether humanity remains capable of leading what it creates. Humans + Machines, under human leadership.

items.title: AI Use and Learning Outcomes Among Undergraduate Students: The Mediating Role of Learning Motivation, Locus of Control, and Learning Preferences
items.abstract: Background. The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities for personalized learning, although its contribution to student achievement remains theoretically and empirically contested. Purpose. This study examined the direct and indirect effects of AI use on conceptual understanding and problem-solving ability through learning motivation, locus of control, and learning preferences. Method. A quantitative explanatory design was employed with 88 pre-service teachers enrolled in an Instructional Media course at a teacher education institution in Central Java, Indonesia. Data were collected using validated questionnaires and cognitive assessments. Preliminary analyses were conducted using SPSS, while the measurement and structural models were evaluated through PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. Novelty. This study simultaneously tested three psychological and learning-related mediators within a single structural model, thereby extending previous research that primarily examined the direct relationship between AI use and academic performance. Results. AI use significantly predicted learning motivation and locus of control but did not significantly influence learning preferences. Learning motivation significantly predicted learning outcomes and mediated the relationship between AI use and learning outcomes. In contrast, locus of control and learning preferences showed no significant mediating effects. The direct effect of AI use on learning outcomes was also nonsignificant. Conclusion. AI contributes to student learning primarily by strengthening learning motivation rather than through direct technological exposure. Effective AI integration should therefore emphasize reflective, autonomous, and cognitively engaging learning activities.

items.title: AI-Enhanced Performance Appraisal Systems: Assessing the Interplay Between Machine Feedback, Employee Motivation, and Career Mobility
items.abstract: Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into performance appraisal systems has fundamentally transformed how organizations evaluate, reward, and guide talent. This paper examines the complex interplay between automated machine feedback, employee intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and long-term career mobility within modern corporate structures. Traditional performance reviews, historically plagued by manager bias, infrequent feedback cycles, and administrative lag, are increasingly being replaced by real-time, algorithmic evaluation tools that continuously monitor productivity, communication patterns, and milestone attainment. While these advanced systems offer unprecedented objectivity, data granularity, and operational efficiency, they simultaneously introduce critical psychological and structural challenges for the workforce. The research investigates how algorithmic oversight impacts employee motivation, exploring the fine line between constructive data-driven guidance and dehumanizing surveillance. When machine feedback is perceived as opaque, overly punitive, or devoid of contextual empathy, it can trigger algorithmic anxiety, disengagement, and strategic gaming of metrics. Conversely, when integrated transparently, AI-driven insights can empower employees with actionable developmental pathways, aligning daily performance with overarching career trajectories. The study further analyzes the implications of automated career mobility, evaluating how machine-generated talent mapping influences promotions, skill-gap identification, and succession planning. It highlights the risk of algorithmic bias reinforcing historical inequities, thereby restricting advancement opportunities for diverse employee segments if human oversight is absent. Methodologically, this paper synthesizes contemporary organizational psychology literature with a comparative evaluation of organizations deploying AI-augmented human resource management systems. The analytical framework correlates the frequency and framing of machine feedback with metrics of employee retention, morale, and promotional velocity. The findings suggest that optimal performance outcomes are achieved not through pure automation, but through a hybrid model where AI serves as an objective diagnostic tool that amplifies—rather than replaces—human managerial mentorship and empathy. Ultimately, this study provides human resource leaders and technologists with a strategic framework for designing ethical, motivation-enhancing appraisal architectures that foster sustainable career growth and organizational agility.

items.title: AI-Powered Personalized Learning: Enhancing Student Academic Achievement and Motivation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications have driven education toward more adaptive and personalized learning experiences and environments. By offering educators tools to customize learning paths, adapt resources to students’ needs, and provide tailored feedback, AI applications are able to boost student academic achievement and motivation. This study seeks to assess the impact of an AI-enhanced learning approach on students’ academic achievement and motivation. We employed a quasi-experimental method for this study with a total of 54 sixth-grade pupils at a private bilingual school in Barka, Oman split into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group was taught using AI applications and the control group was taught using the Moodle learning management system. Results of the study indicate that the AI-powered approach significantly increased students’ academic achievement (p < .05) and motivation (p < .01), with notable gains in attention, confidence, and relevance. ’The findings of the study highlight the significant potential of AI to reshape learners’ experiences and enhance learning and motivation by providing adaptive and personalized learning. Given the small sample size and study environment, the generalizability of the results is limited. Future studies should investigate the scalability of AI-powered learning aids across different educational environments.

items.title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
items.abstract: Desk-based learning and creative activities benefit from handwritten engagement. However, current generative AI tools deliver guidance through a separate screen, creating a gap between where users think and where assistance appears. To address this, in this work we design AIfred, a desk-based robotic arm with a projector mounted at the end-effector that places AI-generated guidance alongside handwritten work. AIfred combines workspace perception, context-aware content generation, and robot-mediated projection to support math assignments, image generation, and drawing tasks. In a user study (n = 36), we compared AIfred against ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Luna) running on a laptop. Both tools performed comparably while assistance was available during the math assignment (6.7 vs. 7.3/10, p = .41), but AIfred improved short-term learning transfer by 60% once assistance was withdrawn (7.0 vs. 4.4/10, p = .003). In addition, independent art and design professors ranked drawings produced with AIfred better in 33 of 36 cases. Our findings indicate that spatially co-located AI assistance benefits tasks whose guidance shares a spatial frame with the work.

items.title: Algorithmic Oversight: Caremark's Fiduciary Framework Applied to Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence now drives core corporate decision, such as loan approvals and hiring screens, yet corporate boards have largely treated its governance as a management-level policy questions rather than a fiduciary obligation. This paper argues that this framing is mistaken, using Delaware's Caremark doctrine, as refined by Marchand v. Barnhill, In re Boeing, and In re McDonald's. The relevant cases already impose an enforceable duty on boards to actively oversee mission algorithmic systems, and by applying Marchand's mission-critical standard, this paper demonstrates that AI performs core business functions that expose companies to anti-discrimination, consumer protection, and securities liability. The paper also identifies a structural problem that existing doctrine has not confronted: unlike the legible red flags at issue in Caremark, Boeing, and Clovis Oncology, AI systems generate outputs without human-readable explanations, allowing boards to receive clean compliance reports from systems that are producing unlawful outcomes. This "black box problem" requires reestablishing what good-faith oversight demands and when the underlying risk bypasses traditional reporting structures. Drawing on In re SolarWinds and the officer liability extension in McDonald's, this paper proposes a scalable framework for reasonable AI oversight, including board-level AI audit committees, a Chief AI Officer role with reporting duties to the General Counsel and CEO, mandatory governance disclosure, and a safe harbor for compliance. Ultimately, this paper challenges that the doctrinal tools to govern AI already exist within Delaware law, and all that remains is for boards to act before litigation forces the question.

items.abstract: Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) is a crucial aspect of construction projects, particularly roof rehabilitation work, which carries a high risk of accidents. This study aims to identify hazards, analyze risk levels, and determine risk controls for the Kepulungan Community Health Center Roof Rehabilitation Project using the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Risk Control (HIRARC) method. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed, involving observations, interviews, documentation reviews, and a literature study with 15 respondents. The results indicate that the dominant hazards were falls from heights (100%) with a risk score of 25 (extreme), being struck by falling materials (93.33%) with a score of 16 (high), slips/trips (86.67%) with a score of 12 (high), cuts/lacerations (80%) with a score of 6 (moderate), and electric shock (73.33%) with a score of 12 (high). Implemented controls included the use of Personal Protective Equipment (100%), safety briefings (93.33%), standard-compliant scaffolding (86.67%), safety officer supervision (86.67%), and OHS signage (80%). Workers' perceptions yielded an average score of 4.21 ("agree"), indicating that OHS risk management implementation has been effective. However, improvements in training, supervision of work at heights, and fall protection systems are still required to minimize workplace accidents..

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in Mathematics Teaching and Learning: Opportunities, Challenges and Future Prospects
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing mathematics education through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated feedback, assessment support, and teacher assistance. AI-enabled systems can adapt tasks to learners’ needs, provide immediate feedback, generate practice questions, and help identify misconceptions. Recent reviews suggest that adaptive platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative-AI tools can support engagement, self-paced learning, conceptual understanding, and mathematical problem-solving when used under effective teacher guidance.link.springer+1 However, AI is not a replacement for mathematics teachers. Concerns remain about inaccurate AI-generated solutions, student overdependence, privacy risks, unequal access to devices and internet connectivity, algorithmic bias, and limited teacher preparedness. Evidence also remains mixed, particularly because many studies are short-term and report limited standardized measures of learning impact. This paper reviews the opportunities and challenges of AI in mathematics teaching and learning and proposes a Human–AI Collaborative Framework for responsible, equitable, and pedagogically meaningful implementation.frontiersin+1

items.title: Application of the ELMERI Observation Method for Occupational Health and Safety Performance Assessment in a Manufacturing Plant
items.abstract: Manufacturing workplaces involve hazards associated with machinery, material handling, worker practices, and environmental conditions. This study aimed to assess occupational health and safety conditions and identify priorities for improvement at a water fixture component manufacturing facility in Istanbul, Türkiye. A descriptive assessment was conducted using the ELMERI Observation Method across seven categories. A single researcher conducted observations three days per week from April to June 2021 and recorded 114 checklist-item ratings, comprising 74 correct and 40 incorrect classifications. Category-specific and overall safety indices were calculated from these counts. The overall index was 64.9%. Safety-related behavior had the highest category index (83.3%), followed by first aid and fire safety (71.4%), order and cleanliness (68.4%), and machine safety (66.7%). Lower indices were obtained for ergonomics (50.0%), industrial hygiene (44.4%), and floors and passageways (25.0%). The findings indicate that favorable ratings for observed worker practices coexisted with deficiencies in physical workplace conditions. Priorities included unobstructed passageways, machine guarding, ventilation, and ergonomic improvements. Unequal observation counts, potential observer bias, and the single-facility design limit interpretation and generalizability. The assessment identified practical priorities for the facility; the effectiveness of the proposed corrective actions requires follow-up evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Changing Patterns of Human Social Interaction
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into daily life is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of human social interaction and communication patterns. AI-powered tools, from sophisticated chatbots and virtual assistants to complex social media algorithms, are increasingly mediating, augmenting, and, in some cases, replacing human-to-human communication. This paper explores the transformative impact of AI on how people connect, express emotions, and form relationships. We examine the dual nature of this shift, highlighting the benefits of enhanced efficiency, accessibility, and personalization, while also scrutinizing the profound risks, including the potential for social isolation, the erosion of authentic connection, the creation of algorithmic echo chambers, and ethical challenges such as bias and lack of transparency. Ultimately, the paper argues that navigating the future of social interaction requires a critical balance between embracing AI's capabilities and prioritizing the core human values of empathy, connection, and ethical accountability.

items.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency: the mediating role of organizational learning capability and moderating role of digital literacy
items.abstract: Introduction Strategic and organizational solutions are becoming essential due to the global demand for digital transformation, sustained operational efficiency, and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence adoption on organizational efficiency, with digital literacy as a boundary condition and organizational learning capability serving as a mediator. Methods The study utilized a quantitative cross-sectional survey-based design. A multistage sampling technique was used to collect data from employees working in the Ghanaian banking sector. Data collected from 388 employees from the banks were utilized in an empirical study employing structural equation modeling. Both direct and indirect relationships were assessed. Results The findings revealed that the level of artificial intelligence adoption has a significant and positive influence on both organizational efficiency and organizational learning capability. The results further showed that organizational learning capability has a significant and positive influence on organizational efficiency and partially mediates the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency. Additionally, the results revealed that digital literacy moderates the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency, as well as the relationships between organizational learning capability and organizational efficiency. Conclusion This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that connects the hitherto overlooked linkages between artificial intelligence adoption, organizational learning capability, digital literacy, and organizational efficiency within the banking sector of an emerging economy. By integrating these constructs into a unified model, the study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI adoption translates into organizational efficiency, thereby extending the Resource-Based View in an emerging-market context.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and auditing: Legal and ethical implications for assurance providers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing audit practice by expanding analytical coverage, automating routine procedures, and supporting more continuous risk assessment. These benefits, however, also raise questions about accountability, explainability, professional judgment, data protection, and legal responsibility. This study examines whether AI auditability and oversight design shape assurance professionals’ perceptions of ethical risk, legal exposure, and audit quality in Ghana. Using a quantitative design, the study combines a cross-sectional survey of 180 assurance professionals with a between-subjects vignette experiment. AI auditability was assessed in terms of data traceability, model documentation, explainability, governance controls, role clarity, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) procedures. The experiment compared manual-only auditing, AI-only auditing, and AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. AI auditability was negatively associated with perceived ethical risk (β = −0.456, p < .001) and positively associated with perceived audit quality (β = 0.424, p < .001). Perceived ethical risk was positively associated with perceived legal exposure (β = 0.536, p < .001) and negatively associated with perceived audit quality (β = −0.268, p < .001). Although AI auditability was negatively correlated with perceived legal exposure, its direct regression effect was not statistically significant after ethical risk was controlled (β = −0.092, p = .392). The experiment showed that AI-only oversight was associated with higher perceptions of ethical and legal risk than AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. Because the study measures professional perceptions rather than observed legal events or realized audit outcomes, the findings should be interpreted as evidence about perceived risk and quality. Overall, the results indicate that responsible AI adoption in auditing depends less on automation alone than on auditable governance, meaningful human oversight, and clear accountability.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Global Business Operations: Evidence from Amazon and Implications for Responsible Enterprise Adoption
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an established part of how organizations run their operations, from customer interaction and demand forecasting to logistics, marketing, and knowledge work. This paper examines what that means for global business operations through a documentary case study of Amazon. The study does not collect primary data or measure Amazon's performance independently. It analyzes publicly available sources: Amazon's corporate publications and regulatory filings, reports from international institutions, and peer-reviewed research. The paper keeps a clear line between what Amazon reports having deployed and what independent evidence shows about outcomes. The paper finds that AI can support productivity, personalization, forecasting, automation, and human decision support, but that the effects are neither automatic nor uniform. Drawing on independent studies, it notes that productivity gains can be substantial for some workers, particularly less-experienced ones, while AI can reduce performance on tasks outside its effective capability range. Amazon illustrates how AI can be integrated across a value chain, including recommendations, fulfilment and robotics, demand forecasting, and generative-AI services. The case also shows why adoption needs governance, workforce development, data management, risk assessment, and human oversight. The paper concludes with an eight-step framework for responsible enterprise AI adoption. It starts from a defined business problem, evaluates AI at the level of individual tasks, and draws on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for risk management. It argues that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on organizational readiness and the quality of human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Higher Education under NEP 2020: A Competency-Based Framework for Achieving Viksit Bharat 2047
items.abstract: Abstract AI and ML are rapidly changing higher education by redefining teaching, learning, research, evaluation, and institutional governance. India's National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions a transdisciplinary, technology-enabled, learner-centric, and innovation-driven education system that produces globally competent graduates who can contribute to Viksit Bharat 2047. Despite rising acceptance of AI-based educational technology, equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, digital infrastructure, and curriculum revision for future workforce needs remain problems. This study critically investigates how AI and ML might improve the quality, accessibility, inclusivity, and effectiveness of higher education in India within NEP 2020. It examines the transformative potential of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, predictive learning analytics, automated assessment, academic administration, and research support, using a doctrinal and analytical research methodology grounded in policy documents, government reports, and contemporary academic literature. It also highlights algorithmic unfairness, data privacy, cybersecurity, digital inequality, academic integrity, and ethical issues in the implementation of generative AI. The Competency-Based AI Integration Framework (AI-HE 2047 Framework) integrates digital literacy, critical thinking, interdisciplinary learning, research and innovation, ethical AI governance, and lifelong learning competencies to align AI adoption with the goals of NEP 2020. The methodology helps higher education institutions produce AI-ready graduates for an innovation-driven knowledge economy. The study found that responsible integration of AI and ML, supported by policy reforms, faculty capacity building, institutional readiness, and ethical governance mechanisms, can improve educational quality, employability, research excellence, and India's transition to a knowledge-powered economy under Viksit Bharat 2047.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in the Sports Industry: From Qualitative Recommendations to Implementation Gaps
items.abstract: This book review critically examines Ekaterina Glebova's Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in the Sports Industry: Past, Present, and Future (CRC Press, 2026) through the lens of AI implementation management. While the book offers a timely and accessible overview of AI applications across coaching, athlete training, fan engagement, and stadium operations, it suffers from several fundamental limitations that reduce its utility for implementation-focused scholars and practitioners. This review identifies five critical gaps: (1) the absence of a political economy perspective on how AI reinforces existing power asymmetries; (2) neglect of non-elite sports and the digital divide; (3) oversimplification of organizational resistance and human-AI conflict; (4) reliance on non-peer-reviewed sources and lack of empirical evidence; and (5) raising ethical questions without providing actionable answers. The review concludes that the book serves as a valuable starting point for early-stage AI adoption but fails to offer step-by-step implementation frameworks, lessons from failures, or concrete guidance for resource-constrained organizations. For researchers contributing to this special issue on AI implementation, this review highlights critical directions for future inquiry, including maturity models, ROI measurement frameworks, and empirical studies of genuine implementation failures.
